content: Artemisinin derivatives represent a relatively new class of antimalarial drugs that have shown promise in treating uncomplicated falciparum malaria, particularly as resistance to other antimalarial medications continues to rise. These drugs have been evaluated for their efficacy and safety in comparison to standard antimalarial treatments. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of artemisinin derivatives, either as monotherapy or in combination with other antimalarial agents, for the treatment of uncomplicated falciparum malaria. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that administered these drugs orally or via suppository to both adults and children. Trials comparing different artemisinin derivatives and treatment regimens were also considered. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others. Additional information was sought from conference abstracts, reference lists, researchers, organizations, and pharmaceutical companies. The eligibility of studies and their methodological quality were independently assessed by two reviewers, and data were extracted accordingly. The review included 41 trials involving over 5,000 patients. However, variations in study design and quality posed challenges for data synthesis. Adequate allocation concealment was reported in only two trials. Most of the data originated from regions in South-East Asia where multidrug-resistant falciparum malaria is prevalent. Artemisinin derivatives demonstrated rapid parasite clearance and high cure rates during follow-up, provided the treatment duration was sufficient. When combined with mefloquine, these drugs showed improved sustained parasite clearance, particularly in areas with multidrug resistance. This combination therapy also allowed for a shorter treatment duration when appropriate doses were used. Importantly, there was no evidence to suggest that artemisinin derivatives were more harmful than standard antimalarial drugs over the typical 28-day trial period. The authors concluded that artemisinin derivatives are both effective and safe for the treatment of uncomplicated malaria. There is no evidence from randomized trials to indicate that one artemisinin derivative is superior to another. In regions with mefloquine resistance, combination therapy with an artemisinin derivative appears to enhance sustained parasite clearance compared to either drug used alone. This review summarizes trials conducted up to 1999, and it will no longer be updated as outlined in the What's new section.
